questions.q: Which base case should factorial(n) use so that every call works, including factorial(0)?
questions.explain: The base case is the smallest input, n == 0, not the last number you multiply. With n == 1, factorial(0) calls factorial(-1), factorial(-2)… and ends in a RecursionError. The answer for 0 is 1 (the empty product); returning 0 would make every factorial 0 on the way back up (Notes p.12–13, p.17).
questions.misconception: The base case is 'the last number you multiply' (1), or 0! means 'multiply by 0'.

questions.q: What happens when you run print(length("hi"))?

options.B: It raises a TypeError, because the inner call hands back None and 1 + None fails

questions.explain: length("i") works out 1 + 0 but never returns it, so it hands back None. Then length("hi") tries 1 + None and raises a TypeError before anything is printed. Computing a value isn't returning it: every path that should produce a value needs a return (Notes p.15, p.8).
questions.misconception: Computing (or printing) a value is the same as returning it.

questions.q: In sum_list([4, 5]) from the notes, sum_list([]) returns 0. Where does that 0 go?

options.A: To sum_list([5]), the call that made it, which uses it to work out 5 + 0
options.B: Straight back to the first call, sum_list([4, 5])
options.C: It is printed on the screen
options.D: Nowhere: reaching the base case ends the whole function

questions.explain: A return value goes back to the call that asked for it, one level at a time. sum_list([5]) gets 0 and returns 5 + 0 = 5; then sum_list([4, 5]) gets 5 and returns 4 + 5 = 9 (Notes p.15, p.14).
questions.misconception: A returned value jumps straight to the first call, or the base case ends everything.
